strengths: Introduces a novel, low-cost earphone-based ExG hardware prototype (NeuroBuds) enabling unobtrusive, long-term, free-living physiological data collection, which is a meaningful departure from bulky lab-based EEG headsets.
Contributes a new dataset, DailySense, with 50 hours of free-living recordings and 20 hours of labeled task-specific data spanning five human senses, filling a gap in ExG benchmark diversity.

The physiology-informed multi-band tokenization (PiMT) is a well-motivated and interpretable design choice, grounded in known physiological frequency bands, and is shown via ablation (1/2/4/12-band comparison) and saliency analysis to meaningfully improve performance.

Extensive empirical evaluation: results on DailySense plus four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV 2b), ablations on pretraining components and patch size, LOSO evaluation, cross-subject/cross-session generalization tests, and on-device efficiency analysis on a smartphone.

Consistent, non-trivial performance gains over strong baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba, EEGNet, etc.) both with and without pre-training, and demonstrated scalability of pre-training with more free-living data.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited: the DailySense dataset is not confirmed to be released (still "working with legal team"), and the earphone hardware is a custom prototype, making it hard for others to replicate the data collection or verify results.

Cross-subject generalization is weak (F1 drops from ~87.6% within-session to ~58.6% cross-subject), and in this setting PiMT even underperforms PatchTST on gaze regression, which undercuts the paper's core claim of learning robust, task-agnostic, generalizable representations.

Task-specific labeled subsets in DailySense are very small (up to only 7 participants per sense-specific task), raising concerns about statistical reliability and overfitting for the six downstream tasks.

The filter bank of 12 bands is fixed via heuristic physiological knowledge rather than learned or rigorously justified; some bands overlap in range (e.g., QRS complex 8–50 Hz vs. EEG-beta/gamma), and no ablation isolates the effect of the overlapping/redundant bands.

Comparisons on public benchmarks are restricted to only two strong baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba); more recent self-supervised EEG foundation models mentioned in related work (BIOT, BrainWave, LaBraM/large brain model) are not empirically compared, leaving the significance of gains vs. state-of-the-art self-supervised methods unclear.

The claim of a "task-agnostic" framework is somewhat overstated since the approach still requires task-specific fine-tuning and decoders per downstream task rather than truly zero-shot or unified multi-task inference.

Demographic diversity of the 22 participants is limited and skewed (16 men vs. 6 women, no discussion of other diversity factors), which may limit generalizability of the collected DailySense benchmark.

The reported improvements on public benchmarks (e.g., DREAMER, Sleep-EDF) are relatively modest in absolute terms and sometimes fall within overlapping standard deviations, weakening the strength of the generalization claim beyond DailySense.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel hardware prototype (NeuroBuds) for unobtrusive, low-cost, earphone-based multi-modal ExG (EEG/EMG/EOG) sensing, addressing a real gap between lab-grade and everyday wearable physiological sensing.

Contributes a new dataset (DailySense) with 50 hours of free-living recordings and 20 hours of labeled data spanning five human senses, which if released would be a valuable community resource; also validates signal quality against a research-grade OpenBCI device (0.71-0.76 correlation).

The physiology-informed multi-band tokenization (PiMT) is a well-motivated and interpretable design that decomposes signals into canonical frequency bands rather than relying on a single wide/narrow band, and is shown empirically to outperform 1/2/4-band variants as well as STFT/CWT tokenization.

Extensive and careful experimentation: results on DailySense and four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI-IV-2b), ablations on pre-training components and patch size, backbone comparison (Mamba vs Transformer), frozen-encoder evaluation, LOSO analysis, statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon), on-device latency/memory profiling, and comparison against pre-training on much larger public EEG corpora (TUAR/TUSZ).

Reasonably strong and consistent quantitative gains over multiple representative baselines (SVM, EEGNet, DeepConvNet, TST, PatchTST, EEGConformer, Bidirectional-Mamba) across diverse tasks, with saliency analysis providing some interpretability of which frequency bands drive each task.
weaknesses: The DailySense dataset, which is a core claimed contribution, is not released and its public availability is uncertain ("currently working with our legal team"), significantly weakening reproducibility and the paper's practical impact.

Cross-subject generalization is weak (F1 ~0.58-0.59 vs ~0.88 within-session in Appendix O/Table 12), which undercuts the paper's central claim of learning broadly generalizable, task-agnostic representations; this is acknowledged but somewhat downplayed in the main text.

Dataset scale remains modest (22 participants, as few as 6-9 per public benchmark, up to 7 per DailySense task), and demographic diversity is limited, raising concerns about the robustness and generalizability of the reported improvements.

The term "task-agnostic" is potentially overstated since the framework still requires task-specific fine-tuning (and separate decoders) rather than exhibiting true zero-shot/few-shot cross-task transfer; the encoder architecture (Bidirectional-Mamba) is also adopted directly from prior work rather than a new contribution.

Some of the 12 predefined frequency bands (e.g., ECG-LF/HF ranges borrowed from HRV literature) are applied to short 4-second windows, raising questions about their physiological validity/meaningfulness at this timescale that are not discussed.

Fair pre-training comparison is limited to PatchTST as the only baseline with a tailored pre-training strategy; other competitive baselines (e.g., EEGConformer, Bidirectional-Mamba without PiMT) are not evaluated with equivalent pre-training in the main results, making the size of the pre-training benefit somewhat one-sided in the comparison.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful and unobtrusive earphone-based ExG hardware prototype (NeuroBuds) enabling free-living, long-term multimodal (EEG/EMG/EOG) recording, which is a meaningful engineering contribution.
Curates a new dataset (DailySense) spanning five human senses with both free-living and task-specific labeled data, which could be a useful resource if released.

Extensive appendices with many ablations (patch size, tokenization variants, frozen encoder, pretraining data scale, cross-session/cross-subject, statistical significance tests, on-device latency) show effort toward thorough empirical validation.
The physiology-informed multi-band filter-bank tokenization is a reasonable, interpretable design choice, and saliency analysis provides some qualitative insight into task-relevant frequency bands.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of well-established components (fixed EEG/EMG/EOG frequency bands, patch tokenization à la PatchTST, masked/AE/frequency reconstruction objectives, Bidirectional-Mamba backbone) rather than a fundamentally new representation learning method; novelty is incremental engineering rather than conceptual.

The claimed 'task-agnostic' framing is overstated: the model still requires task-specific fine-tuning with separate classification/regression heads per downstream task, so it is better characterized as a generalizable/transferable representation rather than truly task-agnostic in a zero/few-shot sense.

DailySense is not publicly released (the paper only states the authors are 'working with legal team' on possible sharing), which severely limits reproducibility and independent verification of the central dataset contribution.

Sample sizes are small and uneven — only 22 participants overall and as few as 6–7 participants per specific sense task — limiting statistical power and generalizability of the reported gains, despite the added Wilcoxon tests.

Cross-subject generalization (Table 12, Appendix O) is weak: PiMT only marginally outperforms PatchTST in classification (58.6% vs 58.0%) and is actually worse in gaze regression (7.78° vs 7.07°), undercutting the paper's central claim of learning robust, transferable representations from free-living pretraining.

The downstream tasks are largely coarse binary classifications (rough vs. smooth, sweet vs. sour, floral vs. sour, interesting vs. not-interesting), which is a simplistic proxy for 'sensing across five human senses' and may not reflect meaningful physiological discrimination beyond confounds (e.g., jaw/facial EMG artifacts during eating/smelling).

Signal validation against a research-grade device (OpenBCI) is based on only 2 participants and ~1 hour of data, which is too weak to support claims that NeuroBuds signal quality is comparable to lab-grade EEG systems.
Demographic diversity of participants is narrow (16 men vs. 6 women), which the authors acknowledge but does not prevent overgeneralized claims about 'everyday' or population-level ExG sensing.

Improvements on public benchmarks (Table 2) are modest in absolute terms (a few points of F1), and only two baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba) are compared there, omitting other established EEG foundation models (e.g., BIOT, BrainWave, Neuro-GPT) mentioned in related work, weakening the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

Potential confound between the effect of pretraining and the effect of PiMT tokenization: much of the reported gain (from 81.9% to 87.6%) comes from pretraining rather than the tokenization scheme itself, yet the abstract and title emphasize PiMT as the central innovation.

strengths: Introduces NeuroBuds, a low-cost ($80), lightweight (20g) earphone-based ExG sensing prototype capable of capturing EEG, EMG, and EOG signals simultaneously, addressing a real practical gap in unobtrusive long-term physiological monitoring.

Curates DailySense, a novel dataset (50h free-living + 20h task-specific across 5 human senses) that is a genuine and useful contribution to the community, filling a gap in free-living ExG benchmarks.

PiMT tokenization is well-motivated by physiological knowledge (12 canonical sub-bands) and is shown empirically to outperform 1/2/4-band variants as well as STFT/CWT/raw-signal tokenization, with interpretable saliency analysis matching known physiological findings.

Extensive and rigorous experimentation: comparisons against 7+ baselines on DailySense and 4 public benchmarks, ablations on pre-training components, patch size, backbone choice (Mamba vs Transformer), data scale, frozen-encoder evaluation, LOSO, cross-subject/cross-session generalization, on-device latency/memory profiling, and statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon).
The comparison against pre-training on much larger controlled corpora (TUAR, TUAR+TUSZ) strengthens the claim that free-living diversity matters more than raw dataset size.
Clear writing, thorough appendix documentation, and hardware/dataset/method form a coherent, mutually reinforcing contribution rather than a single narrow claim.
weaknesses: Cross-subject generalization remains weak and in the gaze regression task PiMT actually underperforms PatchTST (7.78 deg vs 7.07 deg), undercutting the task-agnostic/generalizable framing to some degree; this limitation is acknowledged but not resolved.

Dataset scale (22 participants) and demographic diversity are still modest, and the paper explicitly states uncertainty about whether DailySense will be publicly released, which is a significant reproducibility concern for a dataset-centric contribution.

The core idea of filter-bank decomposition prior to feature learning is conceptually related to well-established filter-bank approaches in BCI (e.g., FBCSP) and multi-band spectral tokenization in prior EEG work; the novelty is more in careful physiological grounding and integration with patch/Mamba pipelines than in a fundamentally new mechanism.

The six reconstruction pre-training objectives and their loss weights are selected heuristically rather than through systematic tuning, and the ablation shows the gains from most individual components are fairly modest (all ablations near 0.87 vs. 0.876 full model), raising questions about how essential each piece truly is.

Gains on some public benchmarks are relatively small in absolute terms (e.g., DREAMER 0.910 vs 0.889 PatchTST), and it is unclear whether these differences are practically meaningful beyond statistical significance.

Efficiency/on-device evaluation substitutes Mamba with a Transformer of similar size due to lack of Android support, meaning the actual real-time performance of the proposed Mamba-based PiMT on-device is not directly demonstrated.
